subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are angles of a triangle, then prove that sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) − sin²(C/2) = 1 − 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) sin(C/2).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.40 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 27.2, on a ★★★ SSP (Super Scoring Page). recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. Same halved condition as the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question — the difference between the two proofs is one sign, not one method.
steps.memory_tip: Same halved condition as the all-plus version — the difference between the proofs is one SIGN, not the method.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof uses, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three squared terms will not factorise as they stand, so one of them is written as 1 − cos² to make a sin² − cos² pair appear. Quote every formula you use in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Keep the minus in front of sin²(C/2); converting the wrong term gives a sum of squares instead.

recall.must_convey: That one squared term is converted to 1 − cos² so a difference of squares appears, leaving the 1 the answer needs.
accept: convert sin squared B over two to one minus cos squared so a difference of squares appears
make a one by rewriting one of the squares
replace the second term with one minus cosine squared
rendo term ni one minus cos square ga marchali
turn one square into one minus the other square

steps.why: The 1 on the right-hand side has to come from somewhere. Converting a sin² into 1 − cos² is where it comes from, exactly as in the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question.
common_mistakes: Converting the wrong term and getting a sum of squares instead.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition is used: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: This version's identity carries a leading minus, unlike the all-plus sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) version's. And cos(90° − C/2) = sin(C/2).

recall.must_convey: That sin²A − cos²B = −cos(A+B)cos(A−B) is applied, and cos((A+B)/2) becomes sin(C/2).
accept: use sin squared minus cos squared equals minus cos of the sum times cos of the difference then convert to sin C over two
apply the identity and use the halved condition
cos of ninety minus C over two is sin C over two
identity apply chesi, cos ninety minus C by two ni sin C by two ga marchali
convert the half angle sum

steps.why: Note the identity carries its own minus sign here, where the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question had none. Missing it flips the whole answer.
common_mistakes: Using the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question’s identity, which has no leading minus.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: The bracket must come out as a SUM so the cosine formula applies. Keep the leading 1.

recall.must_convey: That sin(C/2) is factored out and the bracket becomes a SUM of two cosines — not a difference, as in the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question.
accept: take sin C over two common and the bracket becomes a sum of two cosines
factor out sin C over two, the bracket adds this time
the bracket is cos A minus B over two plus cos A plus B over two
sin C by two common teeste bracket lo sum vasthundi
this time the bracket is a sum not a difference

steps.why: The minus in the question became a plus inside the bracket. That is the single structural difference from the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question, and it decides the final formula.
common_mistakes: Writing a difference and finishing with sines instead of cosines.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity is complete. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see the proof finished.
steps.memory_tip: Use the sum formula to finish with cosines, and do not lose the leading 1.

recall.must_convey: That the SUM of the two cosines becomes 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2), giving 1 − 2 cos(A/2) cos(B/2) sin(C/2).
accept: the sum of cosines gives two cos A over two cos B over two so the answer has cosines not sines
apply the cosine sum formula to get two cos half A cos half B
the bracket becomes two cos A by two cos B by two
cos sum formula tho two cos A by two cos B by two vasthundi
the answer is one minus two cos half A cos half B sin half C

steps.why: A sum of cosines gives cosines; a difference gives sines. That is the whole reason this answer has cos(A/2)cos(B/2) where the sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) question had sin(A/2)sin(B/2).
common_mistakes: Using the difference formula and finishing with sines.

insider_note: One squared sine is subtracted, so the identity needed is sin²A − cos²B = −cos(A+B)cos(A−B), leading minus included. Everything after that follows the usual pattern.
